newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine bank head offers to help new reform chief.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine bank head offers to help new reform chief.

text.p: Ukraine's powerful central bank chief, Viktor Yushchenko, on Thursday gave his full backing to the Serhiy Typhko, the young banker with no government experience put in charge of economic reforms in the cabinet.

Yushchenko, seen in the West as a guardian of reforms in the former Soviet republic of 51 million, told reporters he hoped Tyhypko, 37, would play a positive role in his new post as deputy prime minister.
Tyhypko had been given "a very tough job at a very crucial time when the economic sector is out of balance and in chaos," Yushchenko said.
"The economic bloc in the government really needs a "father" to bring everything together. Of course I wish him success, success, success," he said.
Tyhypko was head of Privatbank, one of the top five in Ukraine and has a reputation as an energetic manager who is able to delegate.
His predecessor was Viktor Pynzenyk, who worked such long hours trying to pull Ukraine out of a five-year decline since independence that he sometimes slept in his office.
Pynzenyk, bitter at the slow pace of reforms, bucked a trend of ministers being sacked by President Leonid Kuchma in recent months by resigning himself.
He had been trying to win approval from the conservative parliament for a tough tax package which would have fought corruption and reined in monopolies.

Western economists have been worried by Pynzenyk's departure and have warned that reforms have stalled so badly that Ukraine could face losing its status as the third largest recipient of U.S. aid after Israel and Egypt.
Kuchma himself has repeatedly slammed the government and Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko in particular for their failure to get approval for this year's budget.

As part of what Kuchma says is a campaign to reduce the number of government officials and make their work more efficient, he has sacked a string of ministers in recent months and more changes in the cabinet structures are expected.
The moves are seen as part of a wider campaign to cut back on bureaucracy and therefore on opportunities for corruption among officials.
Pynzenyk himself accused government officials of worrying too much about their own pockets to approve his tax reforms.
Many foreign investors have complained of widespread corruption in Ukraine and repeated obstacles being put in their way as they try to get businesses going.
Pynzenyk accused parliament and the government of lacking the political will to approve the budget, in legislative limbo between the two branches of power.

The package is on a long list of conditions for Ukraine to win a new $2.5 to $3 billion International Monetary Fund (IMF) loan, and it would underpin this year's budget without which Ukraine can forget about IMF cash.
Washington, keen to prolong Ukraine's five years of independence from Moscow, has been Kiev's main backer at international lending bodies, diplomats say.
